**Explanation:**
According to the provided background, gaining new ideas from a good story does not have to mean learning strictly factual information; it can also relate to "a deeper understanding of human nature, cultural insights, unique viewpoints, or even the exploration of new ideas and themes." 

Through this story, an average reader gains a unique viewpoint and a profound insight into human nature. Specifically, the story explores how physical, repetitive labor—represented by the cold, wet cable of the hand-operated ferry that "wanted nothing from her except hands"—can serve as an emotional anchor and a refuge from grief (the implied loss of Henning) and the painful complexities of estranged family relationships (her son Jonas). Furthermore, it offers a distinct cultural and atmospheric insight into the quiet, stoic rhythm of rural life along the Elbe river in November, giving the reader a lasting perspective on solitude and emotional self-preservation.
